prompt:
以下はある英語ニュースpodcast記事のFull Story・Point One・Point Twoです。
Point One・Point Twoそれぞれについて、以下6項目を判定してください
(それぞれPASS/FAIL)。

- qa_not_caveat_only: このPointが、研究上の限界・一般化上の注意・免責事項
  だけで構成されていない場合PASS(それらに加えて実質的な新しい内容がある
  場合もPASS。留保だけでPoint枠全体が終わっている場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_full_story_paraphrase: Full Storyの要約・言い換えに留まっていない
  場合PASS(Full Storyの中心的なlogic・結論を語彙だけ変えて繰り返している
  場合はFAIL)
- qa_not_other_point_paraphrase: もう一方のPointの要約・言い換えになって
  いない場合PASS
- qa_explains_why_it_matters: 「だから何なのか」を具体的に説明できている
  場合PASS(聞き手にとっての具体的な意味・示唆がある場合)
- qa_specific_not_generic: この記事のLedger固有の内容に基づいており、他の
  どんな記事にもほぼそのまま流用できる一般論になっていない場合PASS
- qa_adds_new_value: 新しい理解・解釈・意外性・具体的示唆のいずれかを
  実際に加えている場合PASS(Full Storyだけを聞いた場合と比べて、聞き手の
  理解が実際に深まっている場合)

reasoningには、判定理由を1〜2文の日本語で書いてください(特にFAILの場合は
具体的な理由を明記してください)。

【Full Story】
Imagine you are reading. Your phone makes a familiar alert. You do not look. You do not touch it. You keep reading. Still, the moment may change your focus. Two peer-reviewed studies tested this hidden problem.

One study tested 73 university students with a simple visual letter task. Some rounds had a notification sound. Others had a neutral sound. The students did not look at or touch a phone. Their responses were slower when the notification sound played.

A second study tested 42 university students with a concentration test and a phone powered off. No notifications arrived. The phone was either on the desk or in another room. Attention scores averaged about 100 on the desk and 109 in another room. Processing speed showed the same pattern.

These results point to two different sources of trouble. An alert may affect the task before a person reaches for the phone. A silent phone nearby may matter too.

A 2018 survey adds a daily-life view. Among 743 US teens aged 13 to 17, 72% said they often or sometimes checked messages or notifications soon after waking. Also, 56% said they felt at least one of three feelings—anxious, lonely, or upset—when they did not have their phone with them. A majority said they felt a need to answer messages quickly. These answers describe this surveyed group; they do not show exactly what caused those feelings.

【Point One】
The first study changes the meaning of “ignoring” an alert. The students did not open a phone, but the alert slowed their next response. The researchers also saw a stronger brain-wave signal that they connect with extra effort to stay on task. They interpret this as the mind using extra control, rather than simply choosing to check the screen.

【Point Two】
The second study suggests a practical difference: removing an alert is not the same as removing the phone from the work space. No alert was delivered, yet scores were higher when the phone was in another room. The study did not measure what people were thinking, but it gives physical distance a clear place in a focus plan.

point_one.reasoning: 通知を無視しても反応が遅くなったという結果に加え、脳波の強まりを示して「確認したい」という意思決定ではなく、注意を維持するための追加努力だと解釈している。これにより、通知を開かなければ問題ないという理解を具体的に修正している。

point_two.reasoning: 通知がなくても机上のスマートフォンが集中を妨げ、別室で成績が高かったというFull Storyの結論を、作業空間から հեռけるべきだと言い換えているにとどまる。実用的な示唆はあるが、Full Storyを聞いた時点で既に導ける内容で、新しい証拠や解釈はほぼ加えていない。
